nameStory: Madagascar Periwinkle gets its name from its homeland - the island of Madagascar off the coast of Africa, where it's found nowhere else in the wild. The 'periwinkle' part comes from its resemblance to the common periwinkle's simple, flat flowers, though they're not closely related. It's also called 'old maid' because the flowers seem to last forever without fading - quite the compliment in the flower world!
description: Madagascar Periwinkle is a tropical flowering plant that's become a popular garden annual in New England. It forms neat, bushy mounds about 6-18 inches tall and wide, covered in glossy green leaves and cheerful flat flowers. The flowers come in shades of pink, white, purple, or red, each with five rounded petals that look like they've been cut from paper. Though it's originally from Madagascar, you'll now see it brightening up flower beds and containers throughout our region during the warm months.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five perfectly flat, rounded petals form a pinwheel shape, often with a contrasting colored center or 'eye' - touch them and they feel smooth and waxy, almost artificial

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem - they feel thick and leathery with a waxy coating that makes water bead up on the surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact, mounded bushes that stay neat without pruning - the stems are sturdy and somewhat succulent-feeling when squeezed

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces narrow, cylindrical seed pods that split open to release small black seeds - the pods point upward like tiny green fingers

habitat: In New England, you'll find Madagascar Periwinkle exclusively in cultivated settings like flower gardens, container plantings, and landscaped areas. It thrives in full sun locations with well-drained soil and cannot survive our winters outdoors. Look for it in parks, botanical gardens, residential flowerbeds, and commercial landscapes during the growing season.

seasonality.spring: Plants appear in garden centers and newly planted beds after the last frost, usually late May or early June, as small transplants with their first flowers already opening.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous flowers from June through September - this is the best time to observe all identifying features in their full glory.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until the first hard frost kills the plants, often producing seed pods in late summer that can be observed into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England landscapes as it cannot survive freezing temperatures - only visible in heated greenhouses or as dried specimens.

funFact: This innocent-looking garden flower is actually one of the most important cancer-fighting plants on Earth - it produces two powerful chemotherapy drugs, vincristine and vinblastine, that have saved countless lives and made it worth more than its weight in gold to pharmaceutical companies.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Impatiens, another popular annual flower, but Madagascar Periwinkle's flowers are completely flat like paper cutouts while Impatiens have pouched, three-dimensional flowers that look more like tiny orchids.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'periwinkle,' this plant is not related to the common periwinkle (Vinca) that grows wild in New England - it was formerly classified in the same genus but moved to its own group. The name confusion persists in garden centers where both are often simply called 'periwinkle.'
compareHints: Madagascar Periwinkle is the only member of its genus (Catharanthus) found in New England. Within the broader Dogbane family, it differs from related Vinca species by having completely flat flowers rather than slightly tubular ones, and thicker, more succulent stems. Unlike hardy Vinca that can overwinter here, Madagascar Periwinkle is strictly a warm-weather annual in our climate.
